followUps:
I cut polish first and keep the spine. With 10 minutes left I stop drawing and spend the time on the one use case that proves the design: the entities, the main operation (park) and its inverse (leave), plus the one pattern the interviewer cares about.

Order of sacrifice: patterns for things that will not change, then edge cases, then diagrams. I say aloud what I skipped, for example: "payment and the display board are out; here is where they would plug in." A running core with named gaps beats a half-drawn complete design.

A 90-minute machine-coding round is judged by running code, so the framework shifts from talking to building. Steps 1 to 4 shrink to about 10 minutes (clarify, entities, signatures), and I skip the full class diagram.

Rough budget: 10 minutes design, 15 for a thin end-to-end slice that runs, 40 adding commands one at a time and running after each, 15 for validation and tests, 10 for cleanup and a note on extension points. The extend step becomes real: I add one requirement in code, not just on the whiteboard.

Usually the pricing rule and the concurrency requirement. If price is per hour with a cap and per vehicle type, pricing becomes a Strategy with a possible Decorator; if it is a flat fee, a single method is enough.

Concurrent gates change the most structurally: they force atomic allocation, locks or a queue of free spots, and a thread-safe ticket map. Single-threaded in-memory is a much smaller design. Persistence is the next one, since it adds a repository interface.

I state my assumptions out loud and write them on the board, then build the smallest version that honours them. Typical defaults: 2 floors, spots of 3 sizes (small, medium, large), vehicles fit the smallest spot that is big enough, hourly pricing rounded up, one entry and one exit, in-memory, single-threaded.

I then name the seams I would open if an assumption turns out wrong (pricing and allocation as interfaces), so a wrong guess costs one class, not a rewrite.

A single class is fine for a throwaway script, a spike, or a problem whose rules will never vary and that nobody else will read, such as a 30-line utility or a quick prototype to test an idea.

The test: will anyone add a second variant, test a part alone, or call it from two threads? If the answer is clearly no, a plain class or even a function is the right amount of design. In an LLD round the answer is almost always yes, because the interviewer will add a follow-up.

Refactor in small steps with tests holding the behaviour in place. First write characterization tests that record what the code does today, with real inputs and outputs.

  1. Replace string types with an enum or class.
  2. Extract the pricing if-else ladder into one method, then into a Strategy.
  3. Move data and the methods that use it together (Ticket, Spot).
  4. Run the tests after every step.

Never rewrite in one go: each step should leave the program working.

followUps:
Yes, but only if the ticket has different behaviour per state, not just a label. For three states (ACTIVE, PAID, EXITED) with two legal moves, an enum plus a guarded method is simpler and I would start there.

State becomes worth it when each state has its own rules: a grace period after payment, a refund state, a lost-ticket state. Then each state is a class with its own pay() and exit(), and the if-else on status disappears. I say this trade-off in the interview rather than adding classes by default.

A Factory helps where the choice of which object to build is repeated or depends on input. Examples: creating the right PricingStrategy from a config value, building the EV-wrapped pricing only for EV spots, or creating spots of the right type while the lot is built from a layout.

It does not help for a single obvious class: new Ticket(...) needs no factory. I add one when I can name the branching it hides, such as if (type == EV) wrap(...) showing up in two places.

code.title: Atomic spot claim: check and mark under one lock
code.python:
import threading

class Spot:
    def __init__(self, id):
        self.id = id
        self.taken = False
        self.lock = threading.Lock()

    # check and mark happen together under one lock, so only one gate can win
    def try_assign(self):
        with self.lock:
            if self.taken:
                return False
            self.taken = True
            return True

def claim(gate, s):
    ok = s.try_assign()
    print("gate %s claims spot %d: %s" % (gate, s.id, "ok" if ok else "rejected, retry"))

s7, s8 = Spot(7), Spot(8)
# both gates looked and saw spot 7 free (stale view), then act one after another
claim("A", s7)
claim("B", s7)   # the re-check inside try_assign stops the double booking
claim("B", s8)   # B retries with the next free spot

followUps:
Keep the free spots in a structure that is already ordered and thread-safe, such as a concurrent sorted set, or a priority queue protected by a short lock, ordered by (floor, distance from entry).

A plain FIFO queue gives "any free spot", not "nearest". With a sorted set, pollFirst() removes the smallest id in O(log n) and hands it to exactly one thread. Released spots are inserted back and sort into the right place. If strict ordering under contention is not required, per-floor queues and "nearest floor first" is a good approximation.

The risk is two threads each holding one lock and waiting for the other's, so both wait forever. Example: gate A locks floor 1 then wants floor 2, while gate B locks floor 2 then wants floor 1.

The fix is a fixed order: always take locks from the lowest floor number to the highest, so a cycle cannot form. Better still, hold only one floor lock at a time: try floor 1, release it, then try floor 2. Keep critical sections short and never call slow code (payment, I/O) while holding a lock.

code.title: Ticket lifecycle: only legal transitions allowed

followUps:
The gateway call is slow and may or may not have charged, so I never assume failure. I retry with the same idempotency key, which makes the gateway return the original result instead of charging twice.

Until I get a definite answer the ticket stays ACTIVE (not PAID), so the driver cannot exit free. If retries keep failing, I show "payment pending", record the attempt, and reconcile later by asking the gateway for the status of that key. Exiting without a confirmed payment is blocked, or an attendant overrides it.

A lost ticket is handled by a separate path: the driver identifies the car by plate number, and a lookup index (plate to active ticket) finds the ticket.

Policy then decides the price: either the maximum daily fee, or the computed fee from the recorded entry time plus a penalty. The attendant verifies identity, the lot marks the ticket PAID with a note "lost ticket", and exit proceeds. This is why I keep a plate index and why entry time is stored on the ticket, not on a paper slip.

code.title: O(1) win check with row, column and diagonal counters
code.python:
n = 3
rows = [0] * n
cols = [0] * n
diag = 0
anti = 0

# X adds +1, O adds -1; a full line sums to +n or -n.
# Time O(1) per move, space O(n).
def move(r, c, p):
    global diag, anti
    rows[r] += p
    cols[c] += p
    if r == c:
        diag += p            # main diagonal
    if r + c == n - 1:
        anti += p            # anti-diagonal
    return n in (abs(rows[r]), abs(cols[c]), abs(diag), abs(anti))

moves = [(0, 0), (1, 0), (1, 1), (0, 1), (2, 2)]
for i, (r, c) in enumerate(moves):
    p = 1 if i % 2 == 0 else -1
    w = move(r, c, p)
    print("move %d: %s at (%d,%d) -> %s" % (i + 1, "X" if p == 1 else "O", r, c, "WIN" if w else "no win"))

followUps:
Because the win condition for K in a row with K less than N depends on neighbours, not on whole rows. A row counter of +3 in a 5x5 board with K = 3 does not tell you that three of those cells are adjacent.

Example: X at columns 0, 1 and 4 of a row has a counter of 3, but no three in a row. So you must check the lines through the last move: count same-player cells in each of 4 directions, both ways. That is O(K) per move, still independent of the board size N.

Undo reverses the exact counter updates of the move you remove, which costs O(1). Keep a stack of moves; undo pops the last move (r, c, player) and subtracts the same player value from row r, column c, and the diagonals the cell belongs to, then clears the cell.

rows[r] -= p; cols[c] -= p;
if (r == c) diag -= p;
if (r + c == n - 1) anti -= p;
grid[r][c] = EMPTY;

Do not recompute from the board: just mirror the addition.

The draw check belongs in Game, not in Board or WinningStrategy. A draw means "the board is full and nobody won", which depends on both the game rule (no winner) and the board state (no empty cells).

Game already orchestrates turns and status, so after each move it asks the strategy "did this win?", and only if not, checks the move count: moves == n * n means DRAW. Counting moves is O(1), where scanning the board would be O(n squared).

Make a NetworkPlayer class that implements the same Player interface, so Game does not change. Its chooseMove() sends the current board state over a socket and waits for the remote reply.

Points to handle: a timeout (a player who never answers loses or forfeits), validating every received move exactly like a local one (never trust the network), and serialising the move as a small message such as "r,c". Because Game only knows Player, a human, a bot and a remote player are interchangeable.

code.title: Undo/redo by reversing counter updates
code.python:
n = 3
rows = [0] * n
cols = [0] * n
diag = 0
anti = 0
over = False
undo_stack = []
redo_stack = []

# apply (sign=1) or reverse (sign=-1) the same counter updates; returns win flag
def apply(m, sign):
    global diag, anti
    r, c, p = m[0], m[1], m[2] * sign
    rows[r] += p
    cols[c] += p
    if r == c:
        diag += p
    if r + c == n - 1:
        anti += p
    return n in (abs(rows[r]), abs(cols[c]), abs(diag), abs(anti))

def play(r, c, p):
    global over
    m = (r, c, p)
    over = apply(m, 1)
    undo_stack.append(m)
    redo_stack.clear()           # a new move invalidates redo history

def undo():
    global over
    m = undo_stack.pop()
    apply(m, -1)
    redo_stack.append(m)
    over = False

def redo():
    global over
    m = redo_stack.pop()
    over = apply(m, 1)
    undo_stack.append(m)

def show(s):
    print("%s: over=%s undo=%d redo=%d" % (s, str(over).lower(), len(undo_stack), len(redo_stack)))

mv = [(0, 0), (1, 0), (1, 1), (0, 1), (2, 2)]
for i, (r, c) in enumerate(mv):
    play(r, c, 1 if i % 2 == 0 else -1)
show("after 5 moves")
undo(); show("after undo")
redo(); show("after redo")
undo(); play(2, 0, 1); show("new move after undo")

followUps:
Because the move list is a history of what happened, and a new move starts a different future. If redo stayed available after a new move, you could redo an old move onto a board that no longer matches it, giving an impossible position.

Example: X plays A, you undo it, then X plays B. The redo stack still holds A. Redoing A now would put a second X on the board, out of turn. So play() always clears the redo stack; the program above prints redo=0 after such a move.

Use a bounded history: when the undo stack holds 3 moves and a fourth is pushed, drop the oldest one. A deque does this in O(1): push at one end, remove from the other.

undo.addLast(move);
if (undo.size() > 3) undo.removeFirst();
redo.clear();

The dropped move still stays on the board; it just can no longer be undone. Memory is capped at 3 move records.

followUps:
The charging meter (or the charging station object) is responsible for measuring kWh, not the pricing class. Pricing only receives a number.

I would define a small interface, for example ChargingSession with start(), stop() and kwhUsed(), implemented by the real charger hardware or by a fake in tests. The exit flow reads kwhUsed() and passes it to the pricing decorator. That keeps pricing a pure function (hours and kWh in, money out), which is easy to test with plain numbers like 15 kWh at 8 per kWh = 120.

An idle fee is another decorator on the pricing chain: IdleFee wraps the current pricing and adds minutes spent plugged in after charging ended times a per-minute rate, perhaps after a grace period.

Example: charging ended at minute 90, car left at minute 110, grace 10 minutes, rate 2: the fee is (20 - 10) * 2 = 20. The charger must report the end-of-charge time, which is one more value from the ChargingSession object. No existing class changes; the factory just wraps one more layer.

code.title: Free-spot queue per spot type: O(1) allocation
code.python:
from collections import deque

# One queue of free spot ids per spot type: allocate = O(1), no scanning
free = {"CAR": deque([1, 2, 3]), "BIKE": deque([10, 11])}

def park(t):
    q = free[t]
    print("park %s -> %s" % (t, q.popleft() if q else "full"))

def release(t, id):
    free[t].append(id)       # O(1) return to the pool
    print("release %s %d" % (t, id))

park("CAR"); park("CAR"); park("BIKE")
release("CAR", 1)
park("CAR"); park("CAR"); park("CAR")

followUps:
After the changes the bottleneck is the shared state itself: the free-spot index and the ticket map are touched by every gate. A single lock or a single database row for "free count" becomes the hot spot.

Next steps are sharding by floor or spot type (each shard has its own lock and queue), and moving slow work (payment, notifications, display updates) off the critical path onto queues. Measure first: if allocation takes 2 microseconds and payment takes 500 ms, payment is the real bottleneck, not allocation.

Give each request a client-generated key (for example gate id plus the plate and an entry timestamp) and store the result under that key. If the same key arrives again, return the stored ticket instead of parking again.

t = tickets.get(key);
if (t != null) return t;
t = allocateAndCreate();
tickets.putIfAbsent(key, t);

In real code the lookup and the insert must be one atomic step (putIfAbsent or a unique database constraint), otherwise two retries could both allocate a spot.

For example the Factory that builds a single PricingStrategy, or an interface with only one implementation and no planned second one. An AI-generated design often has IParkingSpotFactory, ITicketService, IVehicleValidator and so on, each with exactly one class behind it.

I would delete the interface and keep the concrete class, because I can no longer say which future change it absorbs. If a second implementation or a test double appears, extracting the interface later takes a few minutes with an IDE.

YAGNI ("you aren't gonna need it") says do not build for requirements you do not have. It matches the rule here: an interface is justified by a variation that is named or by a test seam, not by a hunch.

The balance: YAGNI argues against speculative abstraction, while the open-closed idea argues for a seam where change is likely. I resolve it by asking the interviewer which things will change, and putting interfaces only there. Everything else is plain code that is cheap to change later.

Sacrifice features first, then tests, and keep validation. A program that crashes on bad input fails the evaluator's checks outright, while a missing optional command is only a gap.

Order I drop things: extra commands and bonus features, then elaborate patterns, then my own unit tests (I rely on running the sample commands by hand), and last of all validation of input, because evaluators love to feed wrong input. I state the cut in the note I leave at the end.

Use the simplest possible parsing: read each line, split on spaces, and dispatch on the first word with a map or a switch. Do not build a tokenizer or a command framework.

String[] p = line.trim().split(" ");
switch (p[0]) {
  case "park": lot.park(p[1]); break;
  case "leave": lot.leave(p[1]); break;
}

Keep parsing in one small function that only translates text to method calls, so all domain logic stays in the classes. Ten minutes at most.
